map.name: script
map.takes: nothing
map.gives: the module ready to use, and a finished map.json when run directly
map.text: script — sets up the tools, the prompt text, and the call counter this decompiler needs, then runs main() when the file is started as a program

children.text: pull in the tools the decompiler needs: ast to read Python structure, json to move data to and from Claude, subprocess to call the claude command, sys and Path for the command line and the file, and jedi to find where each name is defined and used.

hold PROMPT, the full instruction text sent to Claude for every block.
It tells Claude to explain one block of the file as a story: a root line with the block signature, what it takes and gives, and beats that cover the block's cells in order without cutting a statement in half.
keep CALLS, a one-slot list that counts how many times the script asked Claude, so the final report can show the cost of the run.
when this file is started as a program, run main(), which reads the file named on the command line, explains every block of it, and writes the finished map next to the file.

map.name: statements
map.takes: the file path and its source text
map.gives: one depth-and-line-range row per statement, in file order
map.text: statements(path, src) -> list of (depth, start line, end line) — lists every statement in a Python file with how deeply it is nested, so later checks can tell where each statement begins and ends

children.text: Only Python source has statements this can read, so a file with any other suffix gets an empty list and nothing more happens.
Start an empty rows list, then parse the source and let walk() descend the whole syntax tree and append every statement it meets as a depth with a line range.
Give the filled rows back to the caller.

map.name: statements.walk
map.takes: a syntax node and the nesting depth to give its statements
map.gives: nothing back; it fills the rows list of the enclosing statements()
map.text: walk(node, depth) -> None — descends the syntax tree and appends every statement it meets to rows as a depth with a line range

children.text: walk gets a node and the depth its children sit at, and looks at each direct child of that node in turn.
When the child is a statement, record it in rows as the current depth plus its first and last line, then walk into it at depth + 1, because everything inside a statement is one level deeper.

When the child is not a statement — an expression or another wrapper node — walk into it at the same depth, so parts that are not statements do not add a level.
This is what lets a statement buried inside an expression still land at the depth of the statement that holds it.

map.name: cells_of
map.takes: the file path, its source text, and its lines
map.gives: the cells of the file, each one line range, in file order
map.text: cells_of(path, src, lines) -> list of cells — cuts the file into the smallest groups of lines that a later step can explain one at a time, one group per statement's own lines

children.text: start an empty spans list to hold the line runs, and take the AST road only when the file is Python.
hand each top-level statement of the file to emit(), which fills spans with the line runs that belong to each statement alone.
if spans is still empty — the file is not Python, or the parse gave nothing — fall back to blank lines as the cut: every run of non-blank lines becomes one cell, and those cells are the result.

for a Python file, find the lines the statements did not claim: imports at the top, blank-line gaps, anything between statements.
Walk the file once and collect these unclaimed non-blank lines into extra as runs.
give every unclaimed run to a neighbour span: pull the start of the next span back over the run, or, when no span follows, push the last span's end forward. No non-blank line is left out.
return the spans in file order, each one wrapped as a cell.

map.name: cells_of.kids_of
map.takes: an AST node
map.gives: the statement children below it, in source order
map.text: kids_of(node) -> list of ast.stmt — collects the statements directly under a node, reaching through non-statement wrappers to find them

children.text: start an empty out list that will hold the statement children of node

look at every direct child of node: a child that is a statement goes into out as it is, and a child that is not a statement (an expression, a comparison, a comprehension) is opened with kids_of again so the statements hidden inside it join the list too.
This is why a body that sits under an if test or a with item still reports its statements to the caller.
give back the collected statements; an empty list tells the caller that node holds no statement below it

map.name: cells_of.emit
map.takes: one statement node of the file
map.gives: line runs appended to the shared spans list, one group per statement
map.text: emit(node) -> nothing, it fills spans — walks one statement and its nested statements and records, for each, the line runs that belong to it alone

children.text: take one statement and ask kids_of for the statements nested inside it.
a statement with nothing nested inside it is already one cell: record its whole line range and stop.

for a statement that holds other statements, mark every line the nested statements occupy as covered, and emit each of them so they record their own runs.
This is what makes a nested statement a cell of its own instead of a part of its parent.

go down the parent's lines and collect the lines that are the parent's own work: not covered by a child and not blank. Each unbroken run of such lines becomes one span, closed as soon as a covered or blank line breaks it.
This is how a header like a for line, or a line after the nested block, becomes its own cell.
if the last run is still open at the end of the parent, close it at the parent's last line.

map.name: merge
map.takes: a list of [start, end] line spans, in any order
map.gives: the same lines as a sorted list of non-touching spans
map.text: merge(spans) -> list of [start, end] — joins line spans that touch or overlap into the smallest set of continuous ranges

children.text: start an empty result list out that will hold the joined spans
walk the spans from the lowest start to the highest, so every new span can only extend or follow the ones already kept

if the new span starts inside the last kept span or on the very next line, stretch that last span to the farther end instead of keeping two.
If there is a real gap, keep the new span as its own entry.
give back the joined spans, so a caller sees one range per continuous run of lines

map.name: ask_claude
map.takes: a prompt string
map.gives: the parsed JSON object of the model answer
map.text: ask_claude(prompt) -> dict — sends one prompt to the claude command line tool and gives back the JSON object in its answer

children.text: Take the prompt and count this call in the global CALLS counter, so the run can report how many times the model was asked.

Run the claude command as a child process with the prompt and JSON output, and wait up to 600 seconds for it.
If the command fails, stop with the last 500 characters of its error output, because a bad call must not go on quietly.
Read the result field out of the tool wrapper, then cut the text from the first { to the last } and parse it, because the model can put words around the JSON.

map.name: check_block
map.takes: the model answer, the block cells, the statements, the essential lines, and the block label
map.gives: the root object and the beats list, or an assertion error that says which rule broke
map.text: check_block(m, cells, stmts, ess, label) -> (root, beats) — reads the model's answer for one block and lets it pass only if the root is complete and the beats cover every cell in order without cutting a statement

children.text: check_block is the gate between the model and the map: it takes the answer m and the facts about the block, and it either hands back the good parts or raises an error whose message tells the model how to repair the answer.
take the root out of the answer and stop at once if there is no root object.
the root must carry all three fields text, takes and gives, and each one must be a string with real words in it.

for a function block the label looks like name(), so the root text must open with that same signature.
This keeps the root a signature line for its caller and not free prose.
take the beats out of the answer and stop if the list is missing or empty.
at holds the cell number where the next beat must start, and it starts at cell 1.

go through the beats in order. Each beat must start exactly where the beat before it stopped, must end at or after its start and inside the cells, and must have a text that is not empty.
Together these tests make the beats one unbroken run from the first cell to the last.

collect all the file lines that this beat's cells cover, then keep only the essential lines. Blank lines and the header lines of a loop or a branch are not essential, so they cannot make a beat look wrong.

compare the beat with each statement of the block: the beat must hold all of the lines of the statement, or only lines inside it, or none of them. A beat that cuts a loop or a branch in the middle fails here.
The error message lists the cells that are inside that statement, so the model knows which cut to repair.
move at to the cell after this beat, which is where the next beat must start.
after the last beat, at must be one past the last cell. If it is not, the beats stop too early and some cells of the block have no explanation.
all tests passed, so give the root and the beats back to the caller for use.

map.name: carve
map.takes: a line range, the ranges to cut out of it, and the file lines
map.gives: the leftover line ranges, blank edges removed
map.text: carve(a, b, minus, lines) -> list of [start, end] — cuts the ranges in minus out of the line range a..b and gives back the pieces that are left, with blank lines trimmed off each end

children.text:
carve is the tool that gives a block only the lines it truly owns: hand it a range and the ranges that belong to somebody else.
First it flattens minus into used, the set of every single line number that is spoken for.

Walk the range one line at a time, one step past the end so an open run always gets closed.
A line is free when it is inside a..b and not in used; the first free line opens a run, the first line that is not free closes that run into spans. What comes out is a..b with the taken ranges cut away.

Tidy each piece: move its start down past blank lines and its end up past blank lines, and drop the piece if nothing is left.
Without this a block would claim the empty lines that only separate it from its neighbour.
Hand back the trimmed pieces.

map.name: blocks_of
map.takes: the file path, its source text, and its lines
map.gives: the blocks of the file in file order, each with its name, its line ranges, and its syntax node
map.text: blocks_of(path, src, lines) -> list of blocks — cuts the file into one block for each function and class plus a script block for the leftover lines, so each block holds only the lines that belong to it

children.text: Start an empty fns list. It will hold every definition found in the file.

For a Python file, let grab walk the parsed tree and fill fns with every function and class: its dotted scope name, its full line span, and its node.
A file of another kind gives no definitions, and only the script block comes out below.

Make one block for each definition. For each definition, find the definitions nested inside it, then let carve cut those nested spans out of its span.
Thus a parent function keeps only its own lines, and each inner function keeps its lines for its own block.
Cut all definition spans out of the whole file. What is left is the top-level code: the imports, the constants, and the entry lines. If there is any, add it as a block with the name script.
Put the blocks in the order of their first line and give them back, so the caller reads them as the file reads.

map.name: blocks_of.grab
map.takes: a syntax tree node and the list of names above it
map.gives: nothing; it fills the fns list of the caller
map.text: grab(node, scope) -> None — walks the tree under node and adds every function and class it finds to fns, each with its dotted scope name, its full line span, and its node

children.text: look at each direct child of the given node, one at a time, carrying the scope path of names that lead down to this node

a child that is a function, an async function, or a class is a block: start its span at the first decorator line if it has decorators, else at its own line, end it at its last line, and record it under the dotted name that joins the scope path with its own name.
Then go down into it with the scope path made longer by its name, so a nested def gets the name of its parent in front of it.
any other child is not a block, so go down into it with the same scope path: this finds a def hidden in an if or a try and still gives it the correct scope

map.name: calls_of
map.takes: one block, the file's top-level nodes, and the names of all blocks
map.gives: the sorted names of the blocks this one calls
map.text: calls_of(block, body, names) -> list of block names — finds which other blocks this block calls, so the map can draw the call edges and set the layers

children.text:
take one block, the top-level nodes of the file, and the names of every block in the file.
skip lists the node types that start a block of their own, because the calls inside a nested function belong to that function, not to this one.

scope is the dotted path of the block, from outermost name to the block itself, and it is empty for the top-level script code. A name found in the body is looked up along this path, so an inner function sees its siblings first. out collects the hits.

walk the block: for a function or class block walk its own node, for the script block walk every top-level node that is not a definition. Each walk records the block names it finds and stops at the edge of a nested definition.
give back the found names in sorted order, each name one time only.

map.name: calls_of.resolve
map.takes: a bare name from the code
map.gives: the matching block name, or None when no block has that name
map.text: resolve(word) -> qualified name or None — turns a bare name used in the code into the full dotted block name it refers to, by looking outward from the current scope

children.text:
Try the name inside the current scope first, then in each scope above it, up to the file level: join the first k parts of scope with the word and stop at the first join that is a known block name.
This is how Python name lookup works, so an inner call to emit() finds the nested emit of this function before any emit at the top level.
When no scope gives a known name, the word is not a block of this file - a builtin, an import, or a plain variable - so give back None and let the caller drop it.

map.name: calls_of.scan
map.takes: one AST node of the block
map.gives: nothing back; it adds the block names it finds to the shared out set
map.text: scan(node) -> nothing — walks everything below the node and records each name that points to another block, without entering nested definitions

children.text: scan is the recursive search: give it a node and it looks through all the code below that node for names of other blocks, and it puts what it finds in the shared out set.

Look at each direct child of the node, but pass over a nested function or class.
Those lines are their own block, so the names in them are not the calls of this block.

When the child is a bare name, resolve it to the full block name it points to.
If that name is a real block, and not this block itself, add it to out — a name used here is a call to that block.
Then go down into the child and do the same again, so the search finds names at all depths, not only at the top.

map.name: layers_of
map.takes: the blocks and the call list of each block
map.gives: a layer number for each block name
map.text: layers_of(blocks, calls) -> dict of block name to layer number — gives every block a layer, so a block sits one level above the blocks it calls and blocks that call each other share one level

children.text: Start the cycle search: idx, low, on and st are the bookkeeping of the search, comp will hold the group of each block, and k is the counter that gives each block its visit number.

Run strong() from every block that no earlier walk reached, so at the end comp holds a group name for each block. Blocks that call each other in a cycle get the same group, because a cycle has no top and must count as one unit.

Build the call graph between the groups: for each call from a block to a different group, add an edge from the group of the caller to the group of the callee.
Calls inside one group are not edges, which makes the group graph free of cycles and thus safe to measure.
h caches the measured groups, then give each block the height of its group: a block that calls nothing gets layer 1, and each caller gets a layer above its deepest callee.

map.name: layers_of.strong
map.takes: a block name
map.gives: group ids written into the shared comp map
map.text: strong(v) -> nothing — walks the call graph from block v and writes each visited block into comp under the name of the block that starts its cycle group

children.text: open block v: give it the next visit number in idx, copy that number into low as the lowest number v is known to reach, then push v on the stack st and mark it open in on.

look at every block w that v calls. If the search never saw w, go into w first, then pull w's low back into low[v], because what w reaches, v reaches too.
If w is already open on the stack, v calls back into a block the search has not closed, so keep w's visit number as the lower mark — this is how a cycle of blocks that call each other learns it is one group.

if low[v] never fell below v's own number, no call leads back above v, so v is the first block of its group: pop the stack down to v and write v as the group id in comp for each block popped.
Blocks that call each other in a cycle come off the stack together and share one id, which is what the layer count later needs.

map.name: layers_of.height
map.takes: a component key
map.gives: the layer number of that component
map.text: height(c) -> int — gives the layer number of one component: 1 if it calls nothing, else one more than the tallest component it calls

children.text: a small recursive helper that measures how high one component stands over the components below it, with the dict h as its memory so each component is measured one time

if the height of c is not known yet, ask for the height of every component that c calls, and store one more than the tallest answer
a component that calls nothing gets height 1, because the empty case falls back to 0
give back the stored height, new or from an earlier call

map.name: nodes_of
map.takes: a list of tree roots, each with optional children
map.gives: a flat list of all nodes in reading order
map.text: nodes_of(tree) -> list of nodes — flattens a tree of map nodes into one flat list that holds every node, roots and all of their children

children.text: Take the tree of map nodes and start an empty list out, the collector that the walk helper below fills.
Give the tree to walk, which goes through the roots and their children in reading order and puts each node it meets into out.
Give out back: one flat list of every node, which lets a caller count or scan the whole tree with no recursion of its own.

map.name: nodes_of.walk
map.takes: a list of tree nodes
map.gives: nothing; it fills the out list of the enclosing nodes_of
map.text: walk(ns) -> None — walks a list of tree nodes and their children in reading order, appending every node it meets to the shared out list

children.text: take a list of sibling nodes and add each one, in order, to the out list that nodes_of collects into
when a node holds children, call walk on them right away, so a parent lands in out before its descendants and the whole tree flattens in reading order

map.name: number
map.takes: the list of block roots, each with its children
map.gives: nothing; it writes an id into every node in place
map.text: number(tree) -> None — gives every node in the map a readable id, a plain number for each top block and a dotted number for everything under it

children.text: Walk the top-level blocks in file order and stamp each one with a zero-padded id like F01, F02, so a reader can name any block.
Reset a counter for the block and hand its children to walk(), which stamps a dotted id on every node below it, so each beat is named under its block.

map.name: number.walk
map.takes: a list of child nodes
map.gives: nothing; it writes an id field into each node it reaches
map.text: walk(ns) -> None — stamps a dotted id on every node under one root, so each child gets a label like F01.1

children.text: a small recursive helper that labels the nodes below one root node t

for each child in the list, step the counter k up by one and write the child's id as the root's id plus that number, so the children of F01 become F01.1, F01.2, and so on.
The counter sits outside the helper, so its numbers keep running for the whole subtree instead of restarting at each level.
when a child has children of its own, walk into them with the same counter, so every node under the root gets its own number no matter how deep it sits

map.name: owner_of
map.takes: the finished map tree
map.gives: a table from line number to node id
map.text: owner_of(tree) -> dict of line number to node id — makes the table that tells, for one source line, which map node holds that line

children.text: Start an empty owner table. It will answer one question: for a line of the file, which text of the map speaks about that line?

Walk the flat list of all nodes from nodes_of, and keep only the nodes with no children.
A node with children gives its lines to those children, so only a leaf is the smallest text over a line: for each span of a leaf, write the leaf's id on every line number in that span.
Give the table back. links() uses it to turn a line number into the node that owns it, and thus to point from the node that defines a name to the nodes that use it.

map.name: links
map.takes: the file path and the map from line number to text id
map.gives: one row for each shared name with its defining text and its user texts
map.text: links(path, owner) -> list of link rows — finds each name the file defines and records which text defines it and which other texts use it

children.text: Start the search for name links. A file that is not Python gets an empty list immediately, because jedi reads only Python.
Make the full path p, open the file with jedi, and start rows, the list of links that this block will fill.
Go through every name that jedi finds in the file, and pass over each name whose definition is in a different module, because an imported name is not a link inside this file.
Find src, the id of the text that owns the line of the definition. If no text owns that line, the name cannot become a link, thus pass over it.
Collect the ids of all the other texts that use this name, and keep a row with the name, its defining text, and its user texts when there is a minimum of one user.
Give the rows back, so that the reader can go from a use of a name to the text that defines it.

map.name: row_of
map.takes: a cell number, the cell, and the file lines
map.gives: one text line that shows the cell to the model
map.text: row_of(i, c, lines) -> string — writes one cell as a single prompt line: its number, its line ranges, and its first line of code

children.text: a cell can hold more than one range of lines, so first join all of its ranges into one text like "12-15, 20-22"
put the cell number, those ranges, and the first code line of the cell into one row, so the model sees which cell is which and what code is in it

map.name: write_node
map.takes: one node of the map tree and the indent for its line
map.gives: the JSON text of that node and of every node below it
map.text: write_node(t, ind) -> string — writes one map node as JSON text by hand, so the fields keep a fixed order and each child nests one step deeper under its parent

children.text: start the node line with the given indent and the node id, the one field every node has
add the fields that depend on the kind of node: a block root carries name, layer, calls, takes and gives, while a beat inside a block carries only its layer
add the two fields the reader always needs: the text of the node and the line ranges it covers
a node with no children is complete here, so close the object and give the line back

for a node with children, write each child with the same function and two more spaces of indent, then put the child lines in a children array inside this node
the recursion is what makes the depth of the tree show as the depth of the indent in the file

map.name: write_map
map.takes: the output path and the finished map
map.gives: the map file on disk
map.text: write_map(path, m) -> writes the map file — saves the finished map as JSON text built by hand, so the links, the terms and the tree keep a fixed shape a reader can follow

children.text:
Put each link row on its own line of JSON text, then wrap the rows in brackets.
An empty list of links becomes the short form [] instead of empty brackets over two lines.
Do the same for the term rows: one row per line, or [] when there are no terms.
Let write_node turn each top-level block of the tree into its JSON text, indented four spaces, and join the blocks one per line.
Glue the file name, the links part, the terms part and the tree into one JSON object and write it to the given path.

map.name: compile_block
map.takes: one block with its cells, the file text, and the meanings of the functions it calls
map.gives: the checked root node of the block, with its beats as children
map.text: compile_block(bl, cells, name, code, lines, stmts, ess, ctx) -> dict — asks the model to explain one block, feeds every broken rule back into the next try, and gives back the block's root node with one child for each beat

children.text: compile_block turns one block into one checked explanation node. It gets the block bl and its cells, the whole file as name/code/lines, the statement list stmts, the set ess of essential lines, and ctx, the meanings of the functions this block calls.

Collect in bstmts the statements that lie fully inside this block, and write them into stext as an indented outline of line ranges.
The model needs this outline because a beat must hold all of a statement or none of it, so it must see where each statement starts and ends.

Build the prompt. The label is the function name with parentheses, or the words for the top-level script code; span is the block's line ranges; row_of writes one row for each cell. All of this goes into PROMPT together with the file, the cell count and the statement outline.
Prepare the retry state: note is the repair text added to the prompt, errs keeps every rule the model broke until now, and m holds the last answer.

Try a maximum of eight times. Each try sends the prompt to ask_claude and gives the answer to check_block, which lets it pass only if the root is complete and the beats cover every cell in order without a cut statement.

Make the node from an accepted answer: the root text with its takes and gives, and the block's lines joined by merge.
If the block has more than one cell, each beat becomes a child node that holds the lines of the cells it covers.
Report how many cells became how many beats, and give the node back. This ends the loop on the first good answer.

If the answer breaks a rule, show the error, add it to errs, and put the last answer, the new error and all earlier errors into note.
The next try sends this repair text with the prompt, so the model corrects its answer and does not break the same rule again.
If all eight tries fail, stop the program and name the block. A block with no checked answer must not become part of the map.

map.name: main
map.takes: a source file path on the command line
map.gives: map.json beside that file, plus a count line on the screen
map.text: main() -> None — reads the file named on the command line, explains every block of it, and writes the finished map next to the file

children.text:
Read the file named on the command line, stop if it holds no text, and build code: the same file with a line number in front of each line.
Every prompt shows the model this numbered text, so the model and the checker agree on what line 42 is.
Cut the file into cells, the smallest groups of lines a text can explain one at a time, and list every statement with how deeply it is nested.

Build ess, the lines that carry the work: the lines of the innermost statements only, with the blank lines removed.
The beat checker compares beats against this set, so a beat can not cut a statement in half.
Cut the file into blocks, one for each function and class plus a script block, find which blocks each block calls, and give every block a layer, so a block sits above the blocks it calls.
Give each cell to the one block whose line ranges hold it, so parts holds the cells of each block.

Explain the blocks from the bottom layer up. Before each one, collect the one-line meanings of the blocks it calls that are already done, and give them to compile_block as context, so a caller speaks about its callees at their level instead of repeating their insides.
Keep each finished root with its name, its layer, its calls and its lines in done, ready to be context for the blocks above it.
Put the block roots in file order, give every node in the tree an id, and build the table that tells which node holds each source line.
Put the file name, the shared-name links and the tree into one map, write it to map.json beside the source file, and print the counts of blocks, texts, links and model calls.
